Cohen further notes that in the second half of the 19th century such protective firmans become rarer in the sijill record, which he interprets as evidence that the steady growth of synagogues and Jewish communal institutions in Jerusalem proceeded without significant Muslim-public disruption — though he cautions, with reference to a contemporaneous al-Nimri family case (document no. 30), that vigilance against Jewish institutional encroachment on Muslim neighbors remained a live concern.

event: Halukah as demographic engine: the Ashkenazi share of the Yishuv rises from ~25% to ~55%, not through political-Zionist conviction (which does not yet exist), but through halukah-supported religious migration — Vilna Perushim (1812+), Hungarian/German Habad (1840s+), Romanian/Russian pogrom-refugee waves (1860s+).

Italian collection mission after Ibn Farrukh extortion. Community borrowed 50,000 grush at 40% interest from Muslim moneylenders as bridge loan; emissaries dispatched to Italy 'to make collections in behalf of the Holy City, which had been reduced to indigence.' Parallel diplomatic channel to Constantinople secured Farrukh's deposition.
quote: Messengers who had been sent to Italy to make collections in behalf of the Holy City, which had been reduced to indigence through the acts of the tyrannical Ibn Paruch.

passages.text: This remarkable occurrence I have taken in extract from a printed document, entitled 'n man, 'The Ruins of Jerusalem,' printed in Venice, in 5388 (1628), in which this event is told circumstantially, and quite at length. The document was written and signed by the chiefs of the Jewish people at Jerusalem, and given as an authorization to the messengers who had been sent to Italy to make collections in behalf of the Holy City, which had been reduced to indigence through the acts of the tyrannical Ibn Paruch.

event: Special fund-drive announced after 'tax collectors flayed them alive' crisis. First steps taken for Istanbul Committee of Officials. R. David Oppenheim and R. Samson Wertheim led European mobilization. R. Mosheh Hakkohen raised 25,600 ducats in Germany — but diaspora failed to mobilize the 60,000 reichstaler needed. Result: creditors burned the Hurva (Nov 1720).
quote: They have flayed them alive… forced to borrow at interest from the strong ones of the land, at forty percent.

passages.text: The situation in the Sephardi community in Jerusalem was also worsening, and intensive efforts were undertaken in the Istanbul community to ease the pressure. In 1711 a special fund-drive was announced, and the first steps were taken for the establishment of the Committee of Officials for Palestine in Istanbul. Among the people who strove to save the Jerusalem community were R. David Oppenheim, R. Samson Wertheim, and Berman Segal. [...] The efforts in Europe to save the Jerusalem community were concentrated mainly in the communities of Vienna, Prague, Metz, Breslau, and Venice. Large sums of money were collected, but they were not transferred to their destination because of the difficulties in the execution of the 'agreement' with the creditors at the beginning of the second decade of the century. The efforts to achieve the 'agreement' were performed by persons in the Istanbul community who were close to the court of the sultan, with Joseph the physician at their head, as is attested by his correspondence with Rabbi Wertheim and the community leaders in Europe from 1711 to 1717. At the beginning of this decade Joseph the physician succeeded in achieving a draft of an 'agreement,' but in the end the matter failed. In his last letter Joseph the physician laid the blame on the European communities, which did not succeed in mobilizing the enormous sum of 60,000 reichstaler (about 60,000 kurus). [...] All the efforts to save the Ashkenazi community came to naught. In November 1720 the creditors burned the Ashkenazi court and its synagogue, and the Ashkenazi community was dispersed.

event: R. Raphael Meyuhas sent on rescue mission to Istanbul after new ruler demanded 91,000 kuruş in 91 days and arrested community official R. Moses Meyuhas. With assistance of rich Istanbul Jews, succeeded in getting central authorities to restrain the local ruler.
actor: Istanbul court intercession via Meyuhas family

passages.text: In the 1720s additional disasters occurred to the Jerusalem community. In 1722 the city was attacked by a severe drought, and in 1723 a new ruler arrived from Istanbul, who made many false accusations and extorted much money. For example, he demanded a payment of 91,000 kurus from the community within ninety-one days and arrested the community official R. Moses Meyuhas. The community quickly sent his grandson, R. Raphael Meyuhas Bechar Samuel—later chief rabbi of the city—to Istanbul on a rescue mission. With the assistance of the rich men of Istanbul the emissary succeeded in influencing the central authorities to arouse the mercy of the ruler. These years saw intensive activity in Istanbul in an attempt to rescue the Jerusalem community from its severe crisis, and in the wake of these activities the Committee of Officials for Jerusalem in Istanbul was finally established.

event: Halukah absorbs Jezzar's 5× cizye increase (4,400→23,650 kuruş). Barnai: diaspora money served 'mainly for payment of taxes to the authorities, for repayment of debts. Only a small part was distributed among the people.' System held until the Napoleonic war broke it.
quote: Money served mainly for the payment of taxes to the authorities, for the repayment of debts… Only a small part was distributed among the people of the community for individual use.

passages.text: In the eighteenth century the lion's share of the income of the Jewish communities in Palestine came from donations from the Diaspora. Every year tens of thousands of kurus arrived in Palestine from individual donors, estates, funds for Eretz Israel in the Diaspora communities, special fund-drives, and the collections of the emissaries. This money served mainly for the payment of taxes to the authorities, for the repayment of debts, and for the running expenses of the community. Only a small part was distributed among the people of the community for individual use. The collection of money was mostly in the hands of the Istanbul Officials, who also arranged special fund-drives in the Jewish communities and sent emissaries from Palestine to supervise them. The large amount of the sums led to waste and often to embezzlements and thefts as well. [Concerning Jezzar's tax policy:] His attitude to the Jews as well was similar to that of Dahir al-Umar. It is true that he displayed a hostile attitude toward non-Moslems, but his desire to develop the region caused him to act fairly to them as long as he gained some advantage from them. [...] Jezzar actually did grant the Jews many reductions in taxes and customs duties, but the war with Napoleon at the end of the century brought about a severe crisis in his relations with the Jews; in this period he needed a great deal of money and he consequently extorted large sums from the Jews.

event: R. Nathan Shapira's emergency mission. Polish halukah cut off after Chmielnicki massacres (1648-49); 400 of 700 Ashkenazi widows died of hunger. Collected 6,000 Reichsthaler + £300 from English Christians via Jessey. Met Menasseh ben Israel in Amsterdam — information used in Cromwell readmission petition.
quote: Sufficient only to pay the interest on principal debts and give gifts to the rulers of the land to extend payment deadlines.
actor: R. Nathan Shapira + Christian millenarian network

passages.text: Yaari documents that R. Nathan (Neta) Shapira b. Reuven David Teveil, a Jerusalem Ashkenazi sage learned in Kabbalah, was dispatched in the mid-1650s after the Chmielnicki massacres severed the customary remittances from Poland-Lithuania to the Ashkenazi kollel in Jerusalem (out of some 700 widows and poor, 400 reportedly died of starvation in 1655). He passed through Venice, reached Hamburg by Kislev 5416 (late 1655) where the Sephardic community pinkas recorded receiving him and the Reichsthaler subsidy voted for him, then traveled to Amsterdam, where he supplied Menasseh ben Israel with first-hand testimony on Jerusalem suffering that Menasseh in turn used before Cromwell's December 1655 committee on Jewish readmission to England. In Holland Christian benefactors organized a parallel collection (extended by Henry Jessey in England, c. 300 pounds sterling), generating a halakhic she'elah to R. Jacob Hagiz in Jerusalem on whether non-Trinitarian Christian donations could be accepted to pay off the community's Muslim creditors; Hagiz ruled permissively be-di'avad given the life-threatening danger. Yaari traces Shapira's return to Jerusalem by Iyyar 5417 (1657), his re-dispatch to Italy that summer carrying the famous R. Baruch Gad Ten-Lost-Tribes letter that became standard emissary credentialing material, his 1660 Venice printings of Matzat Shimurim and Yayin ha-Meshumar, and his death in Reggio Emilia on 1 Iyyar 5426 (1666) at the peak of the Sabbatean movement, with Yaari noting that the Lurianic-Kabbalistic and Lost-Tribes materials he had propagated in Italy helped prepare the ground for that movement's reception.

event: R. Moshe HaKohen's debt restructuring. Multi-year commitments in Hamburg (Billa, mother of Glikl of Hameln, pledged 200 Reichsthaler). On return (1691) negotiated first-ever debt compromise: creditors waived future interest AND one-third of principal.
scale: First debt compromise — ⅓ principal waived

passages.text: Yaari documents R. Moshe HaKohen Ashkenazi's mission on behalf of the Ashkenazi community of Jerusalem in the late 1680s and early 1690s, citing the Verona Ashkenazi community pinkas (11 Kislev 5447 / 1687) authorizing 100 zechinim to be channeled via R. Aharon Voltera of Venice (the appointed Eretz-Israel treasurer) for relay to Jerusalem. Passing through Hamburg in 5447 (1687) Moshe HaKohen secured not only one-time donations but the more unusual arrangement of multi-year and lifetime pledges from wealthy members of the Ashkenazi community; the Hamburg communal archive preserves the subscription list, headed by Bella daughter of R. Nathan Pinkerle (mother of Glikl of Hameln) pledging 200 Reichsthaler annually for Jerusalem's Ashkenazi poor. On his return c. 1690 he found that during his absence the community's debt burden to Muslim creditors had grown further; in 5451 (1691) he negotiated, with the support of Egyptian Jewish leaders headed by R. Abraham b. Mordechai Halevi, an unprecedented compromise (peshara) in which creditors waived all future interest and one-third of the principal in exchange for repayment of the remaining two-thirds within three years. Yaari quotes at length the rabbinic responsum confirming the arrangement, including the Egyptian rabbis' separate decree barring Sephardic emissaries from competing in Ashkenazi territory in Europe for the three-year repayment window, and notes that the Venetian beit din endorsed the agreement before Sephardic factions in Jerusalem subsequently attempted to undermine it.

event: Wertheim-Oppenheim axis. Samson Wertheim (Court Jew of Vienna) sent funds via the Sultan's physician in Constantinople. R. David Oppenheim (Chief Rabbi of Prague, 'President of the Land of Israel') managed the Jerusalem fund. After Hurva destruction (1720), Wertheim family established permanent 'Jerusalem Fund' in Imperial Austrian treasury. Fund lasted until WWI.

passages.text: Yaari documents the Vienna-Frankfurt-Prague axis assembled in 1712 to rescue the Jerusalem Ashkenazi community from its creditor crisis: R. Shimshon Wertheimer (the Court Jew of Vienna), R. David Oppenheim (chief rabbi of Prague, custodian of the 'kupat Yerushalayim'), and R. Yosef the physician at the Ottoman court in Constantinople collaborated to convey a fund (with Wertheimer holding the deposits) intended to negotiate a settlement with the community's Muslim creditors. R. Yosef wrote back to Wertheimer on Rosh Hodesh Kislev 5473 (late 1712) describing his efforts, his summoning of R. Avraham Kafili from Jerusalem, and his pessimism about the chances of success. Negotiations dragged on for years without conclusion; the Metz community withdrew its share after two years when no settlement materialized. The crisis culminated on 8 Heshvan 5481 (1720) when Muslim creditors stormed and destroyed the Ashkenazi courtyard in Jerusalem, burned the synagogue with its forty Torah scrolls, and jailed community leaders. After Wertheimer's death in 1724 the deposits (some 25,000 gulden) passed to his son R. Wolf Wertheimer, who briefly went bankrupt in 1732 after the Bavarian prince defaulted on him but recovered and ultimately returned the full Eretz-Israel deposit with interest. Yaari notes that the residual funds became the so-called 'Jerusalem Foundation' (Jerusalemer Stiftung), deposited in the Habsburg imperial treasury and distributed annually via the Austrian ambassador in Constantinople to Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed until the foundation collapsed with the Habsburg monarchy at the end of World War I.

event: Algazi-Hazan grand mission: 5-year tour of Constantinople, Balkans, Italy. Jerusalem debt at 70,000 lions; interest alone consumed all diaspora donations. Population ~5,000 Jewish souls. Algazi later became Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem.
actor: R. Yom Tov Algazi + R. Ya'akov Hazan

links.label: Same period as Jezzar cizye increase

passages.text: Yaari documents the joint mission of R. Yom-Tov Algazi (born Jerusalem 1727, son of Sephardic chief rabbi R. Israel Yaakov Algazi and member of the kabbalist 'Ahavat Shalom' fellowship at the Beit El yeshiva) and R. Yaakov Hazan (also of Jerusalem, formerly of R. Avraham Meyuhas's yeshiva), dispatched to the Ashkenazi communities of Europe (which by then had eclipsed declining Ottoman Jewry as the principal supporters of the Yishuv) for the six years 1770-1775 to address Jerusalem's mounting debt crisis. The 1770 emissary letter from the Jerusalem sages described the community's debt to Muslim creditors as having reached 70,000 arayot (lion-thalers), explained that even full diaspora donations would barely cover half the annual interest, and noted that the population of Jerusalem had reached roughly 5,000 souls 'in the hands of harsh masters.' The two emissaries traveled via Constantinople (where they printed the appeal letter in 1771 with supporting letters from the pekidei Kushta), Adrianople, Belgrade, and into Italy in 1772-1773, working the communities of Padua, Verona, Ancona, Rome, Lugo, and Casale, granting numerous haskamot (book-approbations) along the way which Yaari catalogues. In Rome they were asked to select a new chief rabbi and two dayyanim for the leaderless community, which they did. Algazi returned to Jerusalem by 1777, was appointed chief rabbi and inherited R. Shalom Sharabi's seat at Beit El; he went out a second time in 1795 in old age and died in Jerusalem in 1802 at age 75. Hazan also returned in 1777 and died in Jerusalem in 1802.

event: Austrian-brokered Hurva debt settlement. Austrian ambassador proposed 30,000 grush from Austrian Jews; Sultan agreed; funds handed to creditors in Jerusalem court as 'final settlement.' Eleven years later a creditor tried to re-impose Ashkenazi debts on Sephardim; qadi ruled against him.
scale: 30,000 grush — partial but accepted as final

passages.text: Cohen 18th sijill at the referenced range describes the 1728 Austrian-brokered Hurva debt settlement. After the burning of the Ashkenazi compound (the Hurva) and the flight of most Ashkenazim from Jerusalem, the Muslim creditors initially attempted to recover their loans from the remaining Sephardi community, which accepted responsibility under a ten-year repayment schedule. The Austrian ambassador in Istanbul then proposed a one-time settlement: 30,000 gurush — funds raised by donations from Austrian Jewry — to extinguish the entire Ashkenazi debt. The Sultan approved, sending an order to Jerusalem instructing the qadi to convene all creditors, register a comprehensive list, and have them sign waivers releasing both the debts and the pledged collateral in exchange for the 30,000 gurush. The transaction was finalized at the Jerusalem court in September 1728 (documents 180 and 1817 in Cohen's numbering). Cohen stresses that this was a singular, ad hoc arrangement, not a precedent. Eleven years later (1739), a Muslim creditor produced a 1707 document asserting joint Sephardi-Ashkenazi liability and tried to compel the Sephardi parnasim to repay 3,600 gold coins his brother had loaned to the Ashkenazim. After consulting the Hanafi mufti of Jerusalem, the qadi ruled in favor of the Sephardim, holding that they could not be charged with Ashkenazi debts — closing the door on further attempts of this kind (document 182).

event: Bayt Mal al-Yahud ('Treasury of the Jews') established — a state institution to collect heir-less Jewish property. Position farmed annually; initially held by a converted Jew 'who knew well the ins and outs of his former community,' then by the Elder of the Jews. Lease prices track demographic decline: 45 gold coins/yr (1550s) → 25 by century's end.

passages.text: Cohen 16th sijill at the referenced range describes the establishment, around the mid-16th century, of a dedicated state-fiscal institution called Bayt Mal al-Yahud ('Treasury of the Jews'). It was created by the Ottoman authorities in Jerusalem to centralize the reporting, supervision, and collection of property belonging to Jews who died without heirs — applying to the Jewish community the general principle that heirless property accrued to the state treasury (Bayt al-Mal). The position of supervisor was annually farmed: the holder paid the treasury a fixed lease price (iltizam) and in return collected the relevant estates. The first known lessees were a converted Jew (documents 64, 65) — Cohen observes that the authorities considered such a person uniquely well-placed to know the internal affairs of the community he had left — after which the role passed to the Elder of the Jews (Zaqen ha-Yehudim), with the position contestable: at one point a Muslim outbid the Jewish elder by offering 25 percent more in lease price and was awarded the role on the spot. Most striking, Cohen presents the lease-price series as a demographic-economic indicator: 45 gold coins per year in the early 1550s, rising to 70 in 1561, dropping to 50 in 1581, and falling to only 25 by century's end (documents 66, 71, 72). He reads the trajectory as reflecting both the declining Jerusalem Jewish population and the diminishing flow of Jewish pilgrims (whose estates were also subject to the institution, document 70) — and concludes that Bayt Mal al-Yahud functioned not merely as a fiscal-legal mechanism but as a barometer of the Jerusalem Jewish community's economic and demographic condition.

event: Rothschild-funded institutions established: hospital, lying-in charity, schools for women and girls. M. Albert Cohn directed the founding on behalf of the Rothschild family. First modern European-Jewish institutional infrastructure in Jerusalem.

passages.text: For in a few days later M. Albert Cohn arrived, a distinguished Israelite from Paris, bringing very large supplies for instant succour of Jewish distress, as well as for establishing permanent institutions — such as children's schools, institutions for manual work, and a lying-in hospital in connection with the hospital already existing. We were informed that some of the funds were from French sources; but a large portion from the Vienna Rothschilds, to whom a letter had been sent describing the efforts made in Jerusalem to meet the distress. A great affair was made of the inauguration of the projected institutions, and others were announced to follow. At the opening of the new hospital, Austrian, Prussian, English, and French Consuls were invited and attended. Speeches were delivered by M. Cohn, who, in his exuberant glorification of France and Paris as 'the centre from which all freedom and civilisation radiate,' contrived to offend the susceptibilities of others of the national representatives present. The speaker even proceeded to decree that henceforth the Turkish Empire was to be revived under the patronage of France. Then, by virtue of his lineage as a priest (Cohn), he mounted on the roof of the new ward of the hospital, and, turning towards the Mount of Olives, and surveying the Jewish wailing place, the great broken arch, and the site of the Temple, he pronounced in Hebrew the Aaronic benediction of Numbers vi. 24. So far so good; but what else? The bigotry of the Rabbis thwarted all his plans — except the hospital and the distribution of alms; — schools, and all that might savour of Gentile education were repudiated, lest they should interfere with 'Holy Gemara;' and his industrial establishments came to nil. Even when Dr. Fränkel, of Vienna, visited Jerusalem the following year, he found no school, and he complains of the want of useful secular institutions. [Cross-reference at lines 11301-11304: 'Besides these, there were in operation the institutions founded the year before by M. Albert Cohn on behalf of the Rothschild family. Among these were the hospital, the lying-in charity, and the schools for women and girls.' — confirming the founding occurred in 1854 and is recalled retrospectively in Finn's 1855 narrative.]

event: Montefiore land purchase outside Old City walls on the Bethlehem road, opposite the Pool of Gihon. Sultan's firman for rebuilding the Ashkenaz Khorbah synagogue. Deed registered in British Consulate and Mahkameh. Planned: almshouses, dispensary, windmill. Founding act of Mishkenot Sha'ananim (completed ~1860) — the first Jewish settlement outside the walls.
quote: A signal favour conceded by the Ottoman Government, on the ground of the purchase being for purposes of a permanent charitable nature.
actor: Sir Moses Montefiore (British subject, sultanic firman)

passages.text: After an absence of six years, Sir Moses and Lady Montefiore now re-visited Jerusalem (July, 1855), with plans for objects more permanent than the distribution of temporary alms. They were accompanied by several friends... We had already learned from the British Embassy that Sir Moses would be the bearer of certain official documents. These he now forwarded to me. They were a Firmân for the building of the ancient Ashkenaz Synagogue, called the 'Khorbah,' and a Vizerial letter, enjoining that aid should be afforded him by the Pashà in carrying out his plans for the benevolent projects which he designed to undertake. On the official presentation of Sir Moses with his documents to the Pashà, a council of the City Effendis was necessary, and had been summoned for hearing the Sultan's Firmân read... The Pasha set the example (which the rest seemed inclined to have omitted) of standing, as usual while a Sultan's Firmân was being read; and of making a salutation of respect at its close... But the principal work was the purchasing of the land outside the city on which to erect the almshouses, dispensary, and windmill. For this object Sir Moses Montefiore obtained a piece of land adjoining the high road going from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, but still opposite the City Walls (on the West), and close to the Pool of Gihon. For this purchase the deed of sale was made out in his own name, though he was not a Turkish subject, and this was a signal favour conceded by the Ottoman Government, on the ground of the purchase being for purposes of a permanent charitable nature. The witnessing, sealing, &c., of the Contract, that is to say the actual Sale, was performed in the British Consulate, but the registration was of course also made in the Public Mahhkameh (or Moslem Hall of Justice). Some of the phraseology of the deed of sale was quaint and curious, as when it makes mention of the permission of the Sublime Government and the imperial throne... and where the purchaser is described as 'Sir Moses Montefiore, Baronet, the honourable person of the Mosaic sect, and ornament of the tribe of Israel (son of Signor Joseph Elijah) who is a nobleman of the Government of England.' By this sale of land to a foreigner and a non-Moslem, another of the remarkable events in the history of Jerusalem was accomplished, of which this year had already seen several — one more step forward in the progress of affairs. Sir Moses and Lady Montefiore, with their friends, at once removed their tents to within the lands so acquired. In a few days afterwards a massive piece of rock, which forms an angle of its boundary upon the road, was marked with the large Hebrew letters [Mem-Mem] signifying, of course, the name Moses Montefiore. And thus was a Hebrew possession once more appropriated in the Land of Promise after an interval of many ages.

event: Hatt-i Humayun (Edict of Toleration) formally proclaimed at the Seraglio in Jerusalem. All Ottoman subjects declared equal regardless of religion. Provision that foreigners may possess landed property. Heads of all religious communities and foreign consuls attended. Finn: 'eminently distasteful to the old Mohammedan population.'
quote: It should be lawful for foreigners to possess landed property.
scaleNote: Enabled all subsequent foreign land purchases

passages.text: WHILE these things were going on in Nabloos, the formal reading of the Sultan's gracious Hatt-i-Humayoon had taken place in Jerusalem. Probably this would have had no effect in preventing the insurrection had it arrived in time to be proclaimed in Nabloos before the riot, which occurred just two days before the Pashà received the document from the Porte. Indeed there were indications that the uproar had been stirred up by people furious at the idea of this edict being granted by the Sultan — as popular report had already informed them. All the leading inhabitants of the country, Moslems as well as Christians, had by this time a general knowledge of its intent. The Pashà announced, on the day after the admission of the great party of travellers and Europeans to the Temple Sanctuary, that on the morrow — April 7 — the formal reading of the Sultan's decree would take place at the Seraglio. That document was justly regarded at the time, and, indeed it ought to be so still, as one of extreme importance — especially by the Rayahs or non-Moslem subjects of the Sultan. His Excellency invited the heads of the various religious communities and the foreign Consuls to be present... I arrived first, in semi-uniform, assigning the reason to the Pasha that it seemed to me best not to make more show lest it should seem that we intended to exhibit a triumph over the Moslem population — thus causing irritation instead of soothing and allaying differences and excitement... We all issued forth to an open terrace, and there the Hatt was read with ceremony in the open air. After that a learned Shaikh of the Noble Sanctuary (Hharam) recited prayers, and acclamations followed from the Turkish authorities, the kawwâsses, and the few Moslems of the town there assembled... A printed copy of the document, in both Turkish and Arabic, was delivered to each Consul, Patriarch, &c. There can be no doubt of this charter of religious toleration and equality having been eminently distasteful to the old Mohammedan population, and distressing to their ancient feelings... Christians were to be no longer brought before purely Moslem courts of justice. Mixed tribunals were to be established, before which the testimony of every one was to be received on oath taken according to the religious law of each sect. Everything that resembles torture was entirely abolished. Christians were to be equally taxed and equally liable for recruitment into the army; and the principle of purchasing exemption was admitted. And finally, it was stated that it should be lawful for foreigners to possess landed property, conforming themselves to the laws and police regulations, and bearing the same charges as the native inhabitants, and after arrangements had been come to with the foreign Powers. These are the most important of the provisions contained in the Hatt-i-Humayoon, or Edict of Toleration.

event: Mishkenot Sha'ananim almshouses completed on Montefiore's 1855 land purchase. First Jewish residential quarter outside the Old City walls. The windmill (still standing) ground grain for the residents. Initially settlers had to be paid to live there — the area was exposed and feared.

passages.text: The Montefiore diaries document the windmill arc directly. At line 2842-2847 Montefiore, on departing Jerusalem after the 1855 visit, promises 'the representatives of the community that he would recommend the committee in London to erect a windmill in Jerusalem, with a view of superseding the expensive method used there for grinding corn. The poor, he said, should then have their flour at a reduced price.' At lines 3260-3272 the diaries record that in preparation for his 1857 (fifth) journey, Montefiore 'made an agreement with Messrs J. J. and T. R. Holman, millwrights of Canterbury, conjointly with the other trustees, for the erection of a windmill in Jerusalem at the cost of £1450.' At line 14238 Montefiore inspects 'the Touro almshouses, the windmill, and the whole of the estate.' The diaries thus directly attest the 1855 promise, the 1857 contract for the windmill, and the completed Touro almshouses (Mishkenot Sha'ananim) inspection. Note: the 'Mishkenoth Israel' society described at lines 14427-14438 is a separate, later (post-1876) Montefiore Testimonial Fund building project, not the 1860-completed Mishkenot Sha'ananim.

event: Alliance Israelite Universelle school founded in Jerusalem. Part of the AIU's broader Middle Eastern Jewish education network (founded Paris 1860). French-language secular education for Jewish children — a direct challenge to the halukah-supported traditional kollel model.
First carriage road in Palestine constructed between Jaffa and Jerusalem. Enabled wheeled transport to the interior for the first time. Precondition for the post-1882 settlement infrastructure.

passages.text: Morris writes: 'The second half of the nineteenth century saw a gradual modernization of the country, accompanying the growing urbanization. While most villages and towns were connected by footpaths rather than paved roads, and people and goods still moved on foot or by horse, camel, or mule rather than in wheeled vehicles, a carriage-road, the first in Palestine, was constructed in 1869 between Jaffa and Jerusalem. The first railroad was laid down in 1892 (also between these two towns), and a second railroad, connecting Haifa and Deraa, running through the Jezreel Valley, was constructed in 1903-05.' Morris places the 1869 carriage road in a broader account of late-Ottoman infrastructural modernization (urbanization, literacy, naphtha-then-electric lighting, the first pharmacy in 1842 and the first European hospital in 1843).

event: Mikveh Israel agricultural school founded by Charles Netter on behalf of the Alliance Israelite Universelle. First Jewish agricultural training institution in Palestine. Trained settlers who later founded First Aliyah colonies.

Mea She'arim neighborhood founded by ultra-orthodox Ashkenazi Jews. Cooperative housing association modeled on European patterns. Second major extra-muros Jewish settlement after Mishkenot Sha'ananim. Named after Genesis 26:12.

Petah Tikva founded by Jerusalem Jews — first Jewish agricultural colony. Land bought from Jaffa Christian Arabs who had purchased from Ottoman authorities after villagers of Yahudiya failed to pay taxes. Abandoned due to malaria; resettled by First Aliyah olim in 1882.

links.label: Part of Zero Aliyah settlement pattern

passages.text: Morris narrates the founding and resettlement at line 784: 'Petach Tikva, the first Zionist colony, was established by Jews from Jerusalem in 1878, abandoned, and resettled by First Aliyah olim in 1882. The original 14,200-dunam-site had been bought from two Jaffa Christian Arabs, who purchased it from the Ottoman authorities after villagers of Yahudiya and Um Labes, its original owners, had failed to pay their taxes. After the Zionists settled there, villagers continued to cultivate fields rented to them by the settlers. They also laid claim to an area of 2,600 dunams, saying that this had never belonged to the Jaffa effendis, and plowed up a road, claiming it ran through their fields...' Cross-cited at Mandel line 2143-2188: 'in March 1886 at Petah Tiqva (the oldest Jewish colony, founded in 1878, then abandoned and resettled in 1882). The Muslim village of al-Yahudiyya, about four miles south of Petah Tiqva, did not have sufficient pasture of its own and used to send its animals to graze on Petah Tiqva's land. The settlers offended the fellahin when they tried to put an end to this practice.' Both authors converge on the 1878-founded / abandoned / 1882-resettled chronology and the Yahudiya land-tax-default provenance of the original purchase.

event: Ottoman government announces Jewish immigrants may settle throughout the Empire EXCLUDING Palestine. Repeated at Ottoman Consulate-General in Odessa, April 1882. Formal onset of the Hamidian barrier. Motivations: fear of 'another national problem' and reluctance to increase foreign-subject population under Capitulations.

passages.text: Mandel narrates the formal onset of the Hamidian barrier directly: 'Thus in November 1881, ostensibly in response to the Anglo-German group's approach, the Ottoman Government announced that: "[Jewish] immigrants will be able to settle as scattered groups throughout the Ottoman Empire, excluding Palestine. They must submit to all the laws of the Empire and become Ottoman subjects." This, in a nutshell, was the Ottoman Government's policy towards Jewish settlement in the Empire from 1881 onwards. In April 1882, it was repeated in a notice posted outside the Ottoman Consulate-General at Odessa, where growing numbers of Russian Jews were applying for visas to enter Palestine, and again in June by the Ottoman Foreign Minister in conversation with the American Minister at the Porte.' Mandel then disaggregates the Ottoman motivation: 'The real reasons lay elsewhere. They were principally two. First, the Ottoman Government feared the possibility of nurturing another national problem in the Empire. Second, it did not want to increase the number of foreign subjects, particularly Europeans and nationals of the Great Powers, in its domains.' He cites Fernandez's report that the ministers were determined 'to resist firmly the immigration of Jews into Syria and Mesopotamia, as they [did] not wish to have another nationality established in great numbers in that part of the Empire' — a fear Mandel grounds in the 19th-c. Balkan-nationality losses and the 1878 Congress of Berlin precedent. Primary citations: Havazzelet xii.41 (1.9.1882) and Levant Herald iii.444 (24.11.1881) for the November 1881 announcement; Ha-Meliz xviii.16 (9.5.1882) for the April 1882 Odessa notice; State Dept. Papers 1882 pp. 516-19 no. 319 (11.7.1882) for the June 1882 American confirmation; PRO FO 78/3394 no. 1155 (30.12.1882) for the Fernandez ministerial report.
